case_study_insert.main_stem: Trailpeak Adventure Park (TAP) is a private limited company in the leisure and attractions industry, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2011 by Ravi Shan, the park operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. TAP plans to invest $640,000 in a new zip-line and ropes course, financed by a $240,000 bank overdraft and $400,000 from a new share issue. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $25 a unit and a selling price of $75, and produces 16,000 units a year, where each unit is one visitor admission. TAP faces long queue times and rising safety complaints, together with a 12% labour turnover among its seasonal ride operators.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Safety Log — Q3 2025: The park recorded 9,500 visitor admissions, with an average queue of 22 minutes at the busiest ride. Safety and queue complaints rose to 31 from 19 last year. Some 7% of rides were idle for scheduled maintenance. An online survey of 2,000 visitors gave TAP a 4.6/5 rating, and 58% said they would return. A skills audit shows 12 of 80 seasonal ride operators have not completed on-the-job training; off-the-job training at the regional centre costs $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Trailpeak Adventure Park as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Leisure Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 5.0% to 5.75%, raising the cost of the $240,000 bank overdraft. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $13.21 to $14.00 an hour, hitting seasonal staffing budgets. (3) Electricity and ride-maintenance input costs have risen 8.3% year-on-year, while domestic tourism spending on attractions grew 5.1%.

questions.question_text: TAP is funding its $640,000 zip-line and ropes course with a $400,000 share issue and a $240,000 bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for TAP of the share issue compared with the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $400,000 that does not have to be repaid and carries no regular interest charge, unlike the $240,000 bank overdraft whose cost rises whenever the base rate moves. For a park with fixed costs of $300,000 a year and seasonal cash flow, this protects liquidity while the zip-line is built, leaving more of the $75 admission price to cover the $25 variable cost and earn contribution.

Point 2: Equity does not require the collateral or daily repayment pressure of an overdraft, so Ravi Shan's new ropes course cannot be threatened by a bank recall if visitor numbers dip below the 9,500 admissions seen last quarter. The share issue also spreads the funding burden among investors rather than concentrating it on a 5.0% to 5.75% interest-rate exposure; although existing owners dilute their control, TAP's autocratic leadership means strategic direction remains clear, and the 4.6/5 rating from 2,000 visitors gives shareholders confidence in demand for the $640,000 expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to TAP's expansion financing.

questions.question_text: TAP wants more visitors for its new zip-line while its 22-minute queues persist. Consider a regional television campaign, local newspaper advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should TAP choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional television: TV would reach a wide audience quickly and could showcase the zip-line visually, supporting the 58% of 2,000 surveyed visitors who said they would return. Yet airtime is expensive for a business with $300,000 fixed costs and an overdraft to service, and many viewers live too far away to visit, so a large share of the spend is wasted.

Local newspaper advertising: Newspaper ads are cheaper and reach the immediate catchment, which suits a park drawing mainly regional day-trippers, and they can carry vouchers to fill quiet days. Their limits are a declining readership and a static image that cannot show the ride experience, so they may do little to cut the 22-minute queues or raise the 4.6/5 rating into more bookings.

Social media influencer marketing: Short video clips of the zip-line and ropes course can go viral among outdoor and family audiences well beyond the local paper's reach. The park already has a 4.6/5 rating from 2,000 visitors and 58% intent to return, which gives credible content, and engagement is measurable against the 9,500 admissions baseline. Drawbacks are that results build gradually and depend on choosing credible influencers, and content must keep reinforcing safety after 31 complaints.

Recommendation: TAP should choose social media influencer marketing, backed by small local newspaper vouchers for off-peak days. It demonstrates the new ride to the widest relevant audience at lower cost than television, converts the strong visitor rating into demand, and reaches further than the newspaper. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for an $640,000 expansion funded partly by overdraft, and newspapers alone are rejected as too passive to showcase a physically thrilling attraction.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to TAP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TAP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in context with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and newspapers are rejected.

questions.question_text: TAP's labour turnover has reached 12% and safety complaints are rising under its autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for TAP of changing to democratic leadership in its workforce of 80.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership would let the workforce of 80, especially the seasonal ride operators, contribute ideas on queue management and ride checks. Being consulted raises job satisfaction and commitment, which should reduce the 12% labour turnover that currently forces repeated hiring and retraining, and helps address the 31 safety and queue complaints by drawing on the knowledge of staff who run the rides daily.

Point 2: Involvement improves the quality of decisions because operators can flag the 7% of rides idle for maintenance before visitors notice, protecting the 4.6/5 rating from 2,000 visitors. Higher morale also supports the 58% of visitors who say they would return: engaged staff deliver safer, friendlier rides, so the new $640,000 zip-line and ropes course can operate smoothly without the disruption caused by constantly replacing leavers. Consultation also fits the park's move away from autocratic leadership, helping Ravi Shan rebuild trust after the 31 safety complaints.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TAP's turnover, complaints, rating and expansion.

questions.question_text: TAP must train 12 of 80 seasonal ride operators who have not completed on-the-job training. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional centre. Which should TAP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the rides is specific to TAP's own zip-line, ropes course and safety checks, costs no course fees, and keeps the 12 trainees productive during the 9,500-admission season. It can directly target the 31 safety and queue complaints and the 7% of rides idle for maintenance. The weaknesses are that trainers are operational staff whose own work suffers, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no external certificate to evidence competence.

Off-the-job training: The regional centre course costs $750 per employee, so 12 × $750 = $9,000, a small sum against the $640,000 investment. It gives structured, certified safety skills and removes trainees from distractions, which matters after 31 complaints. However, it takes 12 of a workforce of 80 away from the rides during peak periods, risking longer queues than the current 22 minutes, and generic content may not match TAP's exact equipment, requiring follow-up coaching.

Decision: TAP should choose on-the-job training as the main method, with short certified off-the-job safety modules later. It is cheaper, tailored to the actual rides and avoids worsening queue times while 12% labour turnover is already disrupting operations. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because the lost shifts would aggravate the 22-minute queues and the generic course would not cover the new zip-line's specific checks. A pilot with one ride group would let Ravi Shan compare complaint counts against the 31 recorded, protect the 4.6/5 rating and check the 7% idle-ride figure before committing the $9,000 fee for all 12 operators.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TAP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of TAP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, queue disruption and safety relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TAP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 16,000 − ($300,000 ÷ ($75 − $25)) = 16,000 − 6,000 = 10,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 10,000 units.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $75 − $25 = $50. Answer: contribution per unit is $50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TAP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. A margin of safety of 10,000 admissions against output of 16,000 shows the park can absorb a sharp drop in visitors and still cover $300,000 fixed costs, guiding how aggressively to promote the $640,000 zip-line.
2. Contribution per unit of $50 lets managers evaluate a family discount: cutting the $75 price to $65 leaves $40 contribution, so they can judge whether extra admissions outweigh the loss before responding to the 31 complaints about value and queues.
3. With 7% of rides idle for maintenance, the $300,000 fixed-cost base and $50 contribution show the admissions needed each day to justify bringing a ride back into service, improving throughput against the 22-minute queue.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $300,000 ÷ 16,000 = $18.75 plus $25 variable cost = $43.75 an admission, against the $750 per employee training spend to assess whether cutting 12% labour turnover lowers costs.

questions.model_answer: (i) Margin of safety = 10,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $50 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: 10,000-unit cushion above break-even; discount pricing from $75 against $50 contribution; maintenance decisions for the 7% idle rides; and unit-cost benchmarking at $43.75 against $750 training cost.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TAP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TAP's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.25 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.36 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.85 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.05 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $40,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $30,000 cash = $125,000; 2025 current assets = $35,000 + $70,000 + $45,000 = $150,000. For 2024, $125,000 ÷ $100,000 = 1.25 and ($125,000 − $40,000) ÷ $100,000 = $85,000 ÷ $100,000 = 0.85. For 2025, $150,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.36 and ($150,000 − $35,000) ÷ $110,000 = $115,000 ÷ $110,000 = 1.05.

Evaluation: Short-term solvency has strengthened on both measures. The first ratio rose from 1.25 to 1.36 even though current liabilities increased from $100,000 to $110,000, because current assets grew faster, helped by cash rising from $30,000 to $45,000. The second measure improved from 0.85 to 1.05 and is the more important signal for a seasonal park: it shows TAP could meet its bills without relying on selling $35,000 of inventories, which is helpful while a $240,000 overdraft and a $640,000 zip-line investment are outstanding. The reservation is trade receivables, up from $55,000 to $70,000, which lock away cash and could weaken the position if corporate bookings pay late, especially given a 12% labour turnover that adds costs.

Conclusion: TAP's liquidity has improved. Both ratios rose and the improvement is not driven by stock, so the park is better placed to meet short-term obligations. Rising receivables remain the main risk, so credit control should be tightened as the expansion proceeds.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on liquidity.

questions.question_text: TAP is considering timed-entry tickets to ease its 22-minute queues. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TAP of this approach.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Timed-entry tickets spread the 9,500 visitor admissions across the day, cutting the 22-minute queue that has helped push safety and queue complaints to 31. Smoother flows protect the 4.6/5 rating from 2,000 visitors and the 58% who would return, supporting the $75 admission price and the $50 contribution needed to justify the $640,000 zip-line.

Disadvantage: Operating a slot system needs booking software and extra staffing at entry gates, adding to the $300,000 fixed costs at a time when a $240,000 overdraft is outstanding. Visitors used to walk-up entry may dislike restricted slots, which could reduce spontaneous admissions and lower the 58% return intention. The insert gives no figure for the software cost or for how much the 22-minute queue deters visitors, so the net gain cannot be quantified and the decision rests on judgement. A timed-entry trial on the busiest ride should be tested against the 31 complaints and the 58% return intention before a park-wide rollout.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TAP's queues, complaints, rating and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.75%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 8.3% rise in energy and ride-maintenance input costs will affect TAP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.0% to 5.75%): If TAP's $240,000 bank overdraft is fully drawn, the extra 0.75 percentage point adds 0.75% × $240,000 = $1,800 a year (0.0075 × $240,000). That is modest against fixed costs of $300,000, though an overdraft is variable-rate by nature so the cost is more immediate than for a term loan. The rise may also make the $400,000 share issue relatively attractive and discourage some discretionary attraction spending despite the 5.1% growth in domestic tourism.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $14.00 an hour): TAP's workforce of 80 includes many seasonal hourly-paid ride operators, so this raises the wage bill and cannot be avoided. The insert does not give hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented. The honest test is productivity: 16,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 200 visitor admissions per worker, so the higher wage is sustainable only if throughput holds or rises; cutting the 12% labour turnover and the 7% idle rides would help maintain that 200 figure.

Energy and maintenance input costs (8.3%): These feed the $25 variable cost on every admission. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only an upper bound is defensible: if the full $25 were exposed, 8.3% × $25 = $2.075, about $2.08 a unit, and at 16,000 units that is roughly $33,200 a year (16,000 × $2.075). Even a smaller exposed share erodes the $50 contribution on each admission, and the effect repeats with every visitor.

Conclusion: The 8.3% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across 16,000 admissions and directly attacks the $50 contribution that funds the $640,000 expansion, whereas the overdraft costs only $1,800 a year on the stated balance and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 200 admissions per worker. TAP should improve maintenance to cut the 7% idle rides and pass part of the increase on through the $75 price.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TAP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TAP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
